SYSTEMVERILOG · COMBINATIONAL RTL · ALU

Parameterized Arithmetic Logic Unit

A single-file, fully combinational ALU whose data width is a compile-time parameter. One 2-bit category select and one 3-bit operation code cover addition, subtraction, bitwise logic, inversion and shifting, with a standard four-flag status output.

Designed by Saket Kumar Jha

Why a Parameterized ALU?

The arithmetic logic unit is the computational core of every processor datapath. Whatever the instruction set, an ALU ultimately reduces to the same handful of primitives: add, subtract, compare, mask, combine and shift. Building it once, correctly, and making its width a parameter rather than a fixed number, is what lets the same block serve an 8-bit microcontroller datapath, a 16-bit peripheral, or a wider custom accelerator without touching the logic itself.

This project implements that ALU as a single combinational SystemVerilog module. Two control bits pick an operation category, three operation bits pick the specific function within that category, and an optional sel line breaks ties for the operations that take only one operand (NOT and the shifts). Four status flags, carry, zero, sign and signed overflow, are produced alongside the result on every evaluation.

Parameterized

One WIDTH parameter resizes the operands, the result, the internal carry-extended temp register, and every flag calculation together.

Purely combinational

The module has no clock and no state. A new result and flag set appear on every change of A, B, control, op or sel, with no pipeline latency.

Flag-complete

Carry/borrow, zero, sign and signed overflow are all derived correctly for both addition and subtraction, not just carry-out.

Control Encoding and Flag Logic

Two-level operation decode

control[1:0] selects a category, and op[2:0] selects the operation within it. This mirrors how real instruction decoders work: a coarse group field followed by a fine function field, which keeps the case statement shallow and easy to extend with a third or fourth category later.

controlCategoryopOperation
00Arithmetic000result = A + B
001result = A − B (two's-complement add)
01Logic000result = A & B
001result = A | B
010result = A ^ B
011result = sel ? ~B : ~A
11Shift000result = sel ? (B << 1) : (A << 1)
001result = sel ? (B >> 1) : (A >> 1)

The role of sel

NOT and the two shifts are single-operand operations, but the ALU always receives two operands. sel resolves which one is actually used, so the same port list serves both one- and two-operand functions without extra opcodes.

Carry-extended arithmetic

Addition and subtraction both compute into a WIDTH+1-bit temp register: {1'b0, A} + {1'b0, B} for addition, and {1'b0, A} + {1'b0, ~B} + 1 for subtraction. The result is the low WIDTH bits, and temp[WIDTH] is the carry (addition) or the inverted borrow (subtraction) — C = 1 means no borrow occurred.

Signed overflow

Overflow can only happen when adding two numbers of the same sign, or subtracting numbers of opposite sign, and the result's sign disagrees with the operands. The RTL implements exactly that rule: V = ~(A[MSB] ^ B[MSB]) & (result[MSB] ^ A[MSB]) for addition, and V = (A[MSB] ^ B[MSB]) & (result[MSB] ^ A[MSB]) for subtraction.

Zero and sign

S is simply the result's most-significant bit. Z compares the result to an 8-bit zero constant; because zero-extension makes an 8-bit zero equal a wider zero of any width, this check is correct for every value of WIDTH, including the 16-bit configuration.

From Truth Table to Verified RTL

  1. Define the operation set. Pick the eight functions (add, subtract, AND, OR, XOR, NOT, shift-left, shift-right) and group them into three categories so a two-level decode is possible.
  2. Design the flag equations. Derive carry/borrow from a carry-extended adder, and derive signed overflow from the sign relationship between the two operands and the result, independently for add and subtract.
  3. Write the parameterized RTL. A single always_comb block with a nested case(control) / case(op) structure, using WIDTH everywhere a bit position or constant would otherwise be hard-coded.
  4. Build a directed testbench. Apply hand-picked vectors that specifically exercise carry, zero, sign and overflow together: max-value wraparound, equal-and-opposite operands, and boundary shifts.
  5. Simulate at the default width. Run the 16-bit configuration first, since it is the module's declared default.
  6. Re-instantiate at a second width. Re-run the identical stimulus pattern with WIDTH = 8 to confirm every equation still holds when operands, flags and overflow logic all shrink together.
  7. Cross-check both runs. Compare the two waveforms operation-by-operation; identical control/op sequences should produce arithmetically consistent, width-correct results in both.

Module Overview

alu_WIDTH_bit #(WIDTH)

The only module in the design. Ports: A, B (WIDTH bits each), control[1:0], op[2:0], sel, and outputs result[WIDTH-1:0], C, Z, S, V. No clock, no reset — every output is a pure function of the current inputs.

Internal temp[WIDTH:0]

One bit wider than the operands, used only by the arithmetic branch to catch the carry-out or the completion of the borrow. Logic and shift results bypass it entirely.

Defaults matter

Every signal is assigned a default at the top of the block (result = 'b0; C = 0; Z = 0; S = 0; V = 0; temp = 'b0;) before the case statements run. This avoids inferred latches, a common and easy-to-miss bug in combinational SystemVerilog, and guarantees a defined output for any control/op combination, including the unused 2'b10 category.

Reading the carry and overflow at 8 bits

10 ns: FF + 01

The largest unsigned 8-bit value plus one wraps to 00 with C = 1 and Z = 1. Since both operands are positive-signed-looking on their MSBs differently (FF is negative as signed), V = 0 — the correct unsigned-wrap, no-signed-overflow case.

50 ns: 00 − 01

Subtracting past zero borrows, giving C = 0 (borrow occurred) and result FF, interpreted as −1 in two's complement, matching S = 1.

110–120 ns: NOT via sel

Same A and B, different result, purely because sel toggles which operand is inverted. This is the clearest single proof that sel is doing its job.

130–160 ns: shifts

01 shifted left gives 02 regardless of whether it arrives via A or B, since the value is the same either way — a useful coincidence that still confirms both the sel = 0 and sel = 1 paths are wired correctly.

The overflow cases the 16-bit run is built around

20 ns: 7FFF + 0001

Two positive numbers add to a negative-looking result (8000). C = 0 since there is no unsigned carry-out, but V = 1 flags the signed overflow correctly — the classic case that separates the two flags.

30 ns: 8000 + 8000

Two negative numbers (by two's-complement convention) add to 0000. C = 1 (unsigned carry-out), Z = 1, and V = 1: negative plus negative should stay negative, so overflow correctly fires.

60 ns: 7FFF − FFFF

Subtracting a negative number (FFFF = −1) from the largest positive number behaves like addition and overflows the same way, exercising the subtraction overflow equation independently of the addition one.

How the two waveforms together validate parameterization

Both runs apply the same category and operation sequence: two ADDs, two SUBs, four logic ops and two shifts, each with representative edge values. The 8-bit run additionally repeats the ADD and SUB pairs to explore more corner cases within its smaller range. Because every flag equation is written in terms of WIDTH and A[WIDTH-1]/B[WIDTH-1] rather than fixed bit indices, the carry, zero, sign and overflow behavior is structurally identical at both widths — the only difference is where the sign bit and the wraparound point sit.

What Changes, and What Doesn't

WIDTH = 8WIDTH = 16Stays the same
Operand range0 – 2550 – 65535Ratio of range to sign bit
Sign bit positionbit 7bit 15Always WIDTH - 1
temp width9 bits17 bitsAlways WIDTH + 1
Unsigned wrap point25665536Always 2WIDTH
Control / op decodeidenticalidenticalCategory and operation logic never changes
Flag equationsidenticalidenticalWritten entirely in terms of WIDTH

This is the practical benefit of parameterization: retargeting the ALU to a new width is a one-line instantiation change, with no risk of re-deriving the overflow or carry logic incorrectly for the new size.

Suggested Visual Elements

1. Control/op decode tree

A two-level tree: control[1:0] branches into three category boxes, each expanding into its op[2:0] leaves, with the active path highlighted as the user picks values from two dropdowns.

2. Live ALU calculator

Two hex input fields for A and B, a category selector, an operation selector, a sel toggle, and a live result plus C/Z/S/V readout computed client-side.

3. Carry-extended adder diagram

A ripple-style block showing A and B entering a (WIDTH+1)-bit adder, with the extra top bit routed out as carry and the rest as result.

4. Overflow truth diagram

A 2x2 grid of sign combinations (A positive/negative x B positive/negative) with the resulting overflow condition highlighted for both add and subtract.

5. Side-by-side waveform comparison

The 8-bit and 16-bit waveforms stacked with a shared time cursor, so the same operation sequence can be compared at both widths at a glance.

6. Flag timeline strip

A compact row of C, Z, S, V lozenges that light up across the full test sequence, making it easy to spot which vectors were chosen to exercise which flag.

7. sel operand-mux diagram

A single 2:1 mux diagram shared by the NOT and shift operations, showing A and B feeding in and sel choosing the active operand before the operator is applied.

8. Parameterization slider

A WIDTH slider (4 to 64 bits) that redraws the bit-width labels on the block diagram and recomputes the wraparound and sign-bit position shown alongside it.
